planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; beesia spreads slowly by rhizomes to form an evergreen to semi-evergreen groundcover mat over two to three seasons.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Beesia is a Chinese woodland groundcover valued for its glossy, heart-shaped, deep-green leaves that stay attractive through most of the year and resist damage from deer and rabbits, making it a reliable evergreen-effect filler beneath shrubs and trees where showier shade plants often get browsed. In late spring it sends up slender, wiry stems topped with small, airy clusters of tiny white star-shaped flowers that hover above the foliage for several weeks before fading, adding a light textural accent without overwhelming the clean foliage mass beneath. It spreads gradually by rhizomes into a tidy, weed-suppressing mat rather than running aggressively, so it fits well among choice woodland companions like hellebores, hostas, and ferns without crowding them out. Keep soil consistently moist, especially through summer heat, and mulch with leaf litter or compost to mimic the humus-rich forest floor conditions it favors in the wild.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-8 weeks before last frost, or sow directly in fall; ladybell forms a long taproot and resents transplanting once established, so set out young plants while still small or sow in place.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to partial sun; ladybell is an East Asian relative of the bellflowers, producing slender, wiry stems clothed in whorled leaves and topped from mid to late summer with airy, nodding sprays of small, pale blue-violet, bell-shaped flowers that bring gentle color to the woodland edge when many spring shade bloomers have finished. The young leaves and shoots are used as a cooked vegetable in Korean and Japanese cuisine, and the thick taproot has a history of use in East Asian herbal medicine, though most Western gardeners grow it purely as an ornamental. Because it develops a deep taproot early on, it establishes best when sown or transplanted young rather than moved as a mature plant, and once settled it is long-lived and easy-care, tolerating light shade and average garden soil without fuss. Deadhead spent flower stems to tidy the plant; it self-seeds modestly where conditions suit it.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, humus-rich starting mix; transplant to a shaded position with a trellis or fence to climb after last frost. Roots take 3-4 years to size up for harvest.

directions: Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with a trellis, fence, or shrub to climb; deodeok, known as sha shen in Chinese medicine, is a twining East Asian vine grown for its thick, aromatic, ginseng-scented taproot, which is a well-known ingredient in Korean cuisine, roasted, grilled, or pounded and seasoned as a savory side dish (deodeok-gui and related preparations) and also used in traditional herbal tonics. The vine climbs by twining stems clothed in soft blue-green leaves and produces distinctive bell-shaped flowers, greenish outside and dramatically mottled maroon-purple within, that hang facing downward through mid to late summer. Unlike its close relative dang shen (Codonopsis pilosula), deodeok's root has a stronger, more resinous, distinctly aromatic flavor that intensifies with the plant's age, and roots are traditionally harvested at three years or older for the best culinary and medicinal quality. Grow it where the deep root can develop undisturbed, and provide support for the twining vine to climb.

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; roscoea emerges late in spring, so mark the planting spot to avoid disturbing what looks like bare soil. Excellent winter drainage is essential to prevent root rot.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Roscoea cautleyoides is a compact, cold-hardy member of the ginger family from the high-elevation forests and meadows of southwestern China, prized for its orchid-like flowers in a wider color range than most roscoea, including soft yellow, cream, white, and pale purple selections depending on the seed strain or named form. Like other hardy roscoea, it emerges quite late in spring and quickly produces a neat rosette of narrow, upright leaves topped by two-lipped, hooded blooms held just above the foliage in early to midsummer, giving an unexpectedly tropical, orchid-like accent to a temperate shade or woodland border. Sharp winter drainage is critical, since the fleshy storage roots are prone to rot in cold, waterlogged soil; raised beds or a gritty soil amendment help in heavier gardens. Combine with hostas, hellebores, and ferns for a layered woodland planting.
